title: Impact of Use of FETL Model in Mathematics Lessons on Student Achievement and Attitudes in Secondary Schools and Postsecondary Institutions in Guyana
venue: European Journal of Teaching and Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Ferreira’s Ecosystem for Teaching and Learning (FETL) Model improves student achievement and attitudes in mathematics instruction. The study is motivated by concerns about low mathematics performance in Guyana and by the need for more engaging, culturally responsive, and technology-rich teaching approaches. The author frames the work around constructivism, the technology acceptance model, and expectancy-value theory.

The intervention used the FETL Model, an instructional framework that organizes lesson planning and delivery around multiple drivers such as student profiles, assessment data, curricula, and learning environments. In the experimental condition, teachers incorporated simulation and gamification tools including Kahoot!, PhET Simulation, Desmos, GeoGebra, Quizizz, and Padlet, and delivered lessons using smartboards and structured FETL lesson plans. Control groups were taught with traditional methods. The study lasted three weeks and included one secondary school plus two postsecondary institutions in Guyana.

The sample included secondary school students and postsecondary students, with achievement measured through pretest-posttest gains and prior term scores, and attitudes measured through a Student Experience and Academic Engagement survey. The results showed significantly higher mathematics progress scores for the experimental groups after controlling for prior performance, and students reported generally positive attitudes toward the FETL-supported lessons. The paper concludes that the FETL Model can support engagement, relevance, and achievement in mathematics across secondary and postsecondary contexts, though the evidence is limited to a short, localized quasi-experiment.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental study with a control group, pretest/posttest data, and ANCOVA controlling for prior achievement, which provides moderate credibility. However, it is not randomized, the sample is small, and the intervention is bundled with multiple components, so causal attribution is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed academic effect on mathematics achievement is statistically significant but modest (partial eta squared = 0.043), below the threshold for medium impact. The study concerns a priority population and promising classroom practice, but the evidence suggests only a modest effect rather than strong impact.

interventions.use_case: Mathematics lessons redesigned with simulation and gamification tools such as PhET Simulations, Desmos, GeoGebra, Quizizz, Kahoot!, and Padlet within the FETL lesson-planning/lesson-delivery model for secondary and postsecondary students.

finding.finding_summary: A quasi-experimental ANCOVA found that students taught with the FETL Model had significantly higher mathematics progress scores than control students after adjusting for previous-term scores, F(1,92)=4.14, p=.040. The adjusted mean progress score was 60.7 for the experimental group versus 52.8 for the control group (n=95 total), indicating a modest but statistically significant gain in mathematics achievement.
finding.measure: Mathematics pretest-posttest progress scores adjusted for previous term mathematics scores via ANCOVA

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive attitudes toward the FETL Model on the Student Experience and Academic Engagement (SEAE) survey across secondary and postsecondary settings. High agreement was especially observed for technology engagement and meaningful/relevant learning items, such as 85.8% agreement that technologies made learning engaging and enjoyable and 92.8% agreement that simulations helped deepen understanding.
finding.measure: Student Experience and Academic Engagement (SEAE) survey; Likert-scale attitude items
finding.study_size: n=106 across secondary and postsecondary participants in survey analyses (reported subsamples included n=28, n=31, and n=47)

finding.finding_summary: The SEAE results suggest positive student perceptions of 4C’s-related outcomes, including collaboration, communication, critical thinking, and creativity, when instruction used the FETL Model. For example, items tied to demonstrating knowledge in ways other than written tests and reflecting on learning received strong agreement, though some collaboration items were weaker (e.g., only 35.8% agreement for enjoying group work in one postsecondary class), indicating a generally positive but mixed durable-skills profile.
finding.measure: SEAE survey items aligned to the 4C’s (communication, collaboration, critical thinking, creativity)
